(15)
satisfies Laplace's equation.
$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { For } \frac{d H_{n}}{d x}=(2 n+1) r^{2 n-1} x V_{n}+r^{2 n+1} \frac{d V_{n}}{d x}, \\
& \frac{d^{2} H_{n}}{d x^{2}}=(2 n+1)\left[(2 n-1) x^{2}+r^{2}\right] r^{2 n-3} V_{n}+2(2 n+1) r^{2 n-1} x \frac{d V_{n}}{d x} \\
& \quad+r^{2 n+1} \frac{d^{2} V_{n}}{d x^{2}}
\end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned}
\frac{d^{2} H_{n}}{d x}+\frac{d^{2} H_{n}}{d y^{4}}+\frac{d^{2} H_{n}}{d z^{2}}=(2 n & +1)(2 n+2) r^{2 n-1} V_{n} \\
& +2(2 n+1) r^{2 n-1}\left(x \frac{d V_{n}}{d x}+y \frac{d V_{n}}{d y}+z \frac{d V_{n}}{d z}\right) \\
& +r^{\cdots n+1}\left(\frac{d^{2} V_{n}}{d x^{2}}+\frac{d^{2} V_{n}}{d y^{2}}+\frac{d^{2} V_{n}}{d z^{2}}\right) .
\end{aligned}$$
(16)
Now, since $V_{n}$ is a homogeneous function of $x, y$, and $z$, of
negative degree $n+1$,
$$x \frac{d V_{n}}{d x}+y \frac{d V_{n}}{d y}+z \frac{d V_{n}}{d z}=-(n+1) V_{n} .$$
(17)
The first two terms therefore of the right-hand member of
equation (16) destroy each other, and, since $V_{n}$ satisfies Laplace's
equation, the third term is zero, so that $H_{n}$ also satisfies Laplace's
equation, and is therefore a solid harmonic of degree $n$.
This is a particular case of the more general theorem of
electrical inversion, which asserts that if $F^{\prime}(x, y, z)$ is a function
of $x, y$, and $z$ which satisfies Laplace's equation, then there exists
another function,
$$\frac{a}{r} F\left(\frac{a^{2} x}{r^{2}}, \quad \frac{a^{2} y}{r^{2}}, \quad \frac{a^{2} z}{r^{2}}\right),$$
which also satisfies Laplace's equation. See Art. 162.
